entry.summary: Visa-free short stays as part of the Schengen area.
entry.max_stay: 90 days in any 180-day period across the Schengen area
entry.pre_arrival: None today. ETIAS is on the watch list.
entry.other: Schengen Entry/Exit System: fingerprints and photo at the border on first entry (free, nothing to do beforehand). Get an entry stamp where one is still given, and carry your passport across internal borders.

tourism.detail: Australian ordinary passports are generally visa-exempt for short Schengen stays, subject to the 90/180 rule.
tourism.next: Confirm the main-destination rule and current border documents.

meetings.detail: Meetings, negotiations, fairs and congress attendance can fit a business visit when no Belgian employment or active local service is performed.
meetings.next: Carry the invitation and state that the trip is attendance/negotiation unless a work route is activated.

conference.detail: Being a delegate or exhibitor is different from delivering paid content, training or production work.
conference.next: Ask the organiser for a role letter and check the Belgian region where work occurs.

unpaid-speaking.detail: A free talk can still be professional activity. Belgium's work and self-employed permissions turn on the actual role, contract and region, not just whether cash is handed over.
unpaid-speaking.next: Send the host exact duties, expenses, benefits and audience for a written classification.

paid-speaking.route: Single permit for employment or professional card for self-employment
paid-speaking.detail: A Belgian employer applies for a single permit; a freelancer or independent professional normally needs a professional card from the competent region.
paid-speaking.next: Choose employee versus independent status before the host books the tour.

book-launch.route: Business visit for rights; regional work permission for launch delivery
book-launch.detail: Publisher meetings may be business travel, while paid readings, workshops, signings, merchandise or local sales can need a permit and tax treatment.
book-launch.next: Split rights, appearance, retail and royalties in the invitation.

ai-teaching.route: Research/academic host, single permit or professional card
ai-teaching.detail: A university invitation can support an academic role, while commercial training remains work or self-employed activity.
ai-teaching.next: Have the institution identify the federal/regional approval and language of documents.

remote-work.detail: Belgium has work and residence permits but no simple dedicated remote-worker route; foreign-work, tax and local-client questions remain.
remote-work.next: Confirm the planned stay and work footprint with the Belgian mission before using visitor entry as a base.

entrepreneur.route: Regional professional card and long-stay visa
entrepreneur.detail: A self-employed founder normally needs a professional card from Brussels, Flanders, Wallonia or the German-speaking Community, followed by the appropriate visa/residence step.
entrepreneur.next: Pick the region and build the economic-interest dossier.

trade.route: Short business visit; local fulfilment needs work/business permission
trade.detail: Trade meetings, sourcing and fairs can be visitor activity; local selling, installation or service delivery may trigger permits.
trade.next: Map the Belgian contracting entity and where the work is physically done.

artist.detail: A performance, exhibition, filming or paid literary appearance should be checked with the promoter and regional authority.
artist.next: Name venue, producer, fee, crew and dates in the host file.

mixed-mission.detail: Belgium's fastest route is often simple visitor entry followed by a regional professional-card or single-permit decision when delivery is real.
mixed-mission.next: Do not let a general Brussels invitation hide the region and employment status.

filming.route: Visa-free Schengen short stay (journalistic or media purposes)
filming.detail: Journalistic or media purposes are listed among visa-free purposes; paid production work and location permits are national matters.
filming.next: Ask the Royal Belgian Embassy, Yarralumla about filming, and the local authority about locations.

research.route: Visa-free Schengen short stay (short-term study or training)
research.detail: Short-term study and training are covered; paid research at an institution is paid activity.
research.next: Ask the Royal Belgian Embassy, Yarralumla if the host pays you.

volunteering.detail: Volunteering isn't addressed in the EU guidance read.
volunteering.next: Ask the Royal Belgian Embassy, Yarralumla.

laws.rule: Laws relating to drugs are similar to those of Australia. Possession of drugs and trafficking of drugs are serious offences.
laws.heading: Drugs

laws.rule: You must carry your passport or a Belgian government-issued ID at all times. It's illegal to wear clothing that largely or completely hides your face in public places (parks, buildings, public transport, on the street). Wearing such clothing risks a fine and/or detention for up to 7 days. There's no exemption for tourists.
laws.heading: Other laws

laws.rule: Belgium has strict rules regarding the importation of goods. You must declare any items that may be prohibited or subject to tax or duty. You're not allowed to bring meat, milk or products that contain these ingredients into the EU. There are some exceptions, including baby food or milk, as well as special food required for medical reasons.
laws.heading: Customs rules

laws.rule: To drive a vehicle, you'll need both: an International Driving Permit (IDP) a valid Australian driver's licence (digital driver's licences may not be accepted). Car rental companies may require both documents. You must be at least 18 years old to drive in Belgium. If you register as a resident with a local commune, you'll need to change your Australian driver's licence for a Belgian licence. money-and-cost.cash_card_notes: Belgium's currency is the Euro. ATMs are widely available. If you're travelling between Belgium and a non-EU country, declare currency of 10,000 euros or more or equivalent. This covers all forms of currency, not only cash. You'll be fined if you don't declare currency or give incorrect information on entry or exit. You don't need to declare currency if you're travelling to or from another EU country.
